3 The steady Navier–Stokes equations

In this section, we deal with steady solutions for the Navier–Stokes equations.
       We first establish the existence of at least one solution for space dimension
       2 and 3. We consider homogeneous and non-homogenous Dirichlet boundary
       conditions. Then we prove the uniqueness of such solution for small data and
       we finally establish asymptotic stability properties of such solutions.

       then we have        (cid:6) (cid:7)                   
                      (v,p) ∈ H2(Ω) d × H1(Ω).

         The solution (v,p) of (V.57) that we found above satisfies the problem
                  ⎧

                    v = 0,             on ∂Ω.                
         Let us first show that v ∈ (Lq(Ω))d for any q < +∞. 
       • In the case d = 2, this property is obvious because the Sobolev embeddings
         (Theorem III.2.34) assert that H1(Ω) ⊂ Lq(Ω) for any q < +∞.
       • In the case d = 3, the Sobolev embedding only gives H1(Ω) ⊂ L6(Ω).
         From this, since ∇v ∈ (L2(Ω))3×3, we deduce that the product (v · ∇)v
         belongs to (L3/2(Ω))3 and thus that we have         
                       f − (v · ∇)v ∈ (L3/2(Ω))3.

From Theorem IV.6.6 applied to Problem (V.61), we deduce that v ∈
         (W2,3/2(Ω))3. By Sobolev embeddings, we conclude that v ∈ (W1,3(Ω))3
         and then that v ∈ (Lq(Ω))3 for any q < +∞.          
       It is now clear that the product (v · ∇)v belongs to (Lp(Ω))d for any p < 2
       and thus that the right-hand side in (V.61) also belongs to (Lp(Ω))d for any
       p < 2. Using once more Theorem IV.6.6, we deduce that v ∈ (W2,p(Ω))d for
       any p < +∞ and finally that v ∈ (L∞(Ω))d.             
         At last, we see that the product (v·∇)v actually lies in (L2(Ω))d. Theorem
       IV.6.6 (see also Theorem IV.5.8) let us conclude that (v,p) ∈ (H2(Ω))d ×
       H1(Ω).
